Greece. Officially the Hellenic Republic, the modern nation-state occupies the eastern Mediterranean peninsula and its islands. It occupies much of the same territory as ancient Greece but with radically different political structures and international status.

From the fall of Constantinople in 1453 until independence in 1821, Greece was fragmented under Ottoman rule. The modern state emerged during the Greek War of Independence and has remained a crossroads between Eastern and Western political, religious, and cultural influences.

Its strategic position in the eastern Mediterranean, the Balkans, and its legacy as the birthplace of Western philosophy and democracy make it geopolitically and culturally significant.

The modern Greek state gained independence from Ottoman rule between 1821 and 1829. It was established as a kingdom with European great-power intervention, marking one of the first successful anti-colonial national movements.

Geography comprises the Peloponnesian peninsula, the Attica region including Athens, and thousands of Aegean and Ionian islands. This makes maritime trade and defense historically central.

The capital, Athens, was revived from Ottoman decline in the nineteenth century. It became the symbolic anchor of modern Greek identity, celebrating its classical heritage as the birthplace of democracy and philosophy.

Greece is divided between Greek Orthodox Christianity, which is dominant, and Muslim Turkish minorities, especially after the nineteen-twenties population exchanges with Turkey. Religious identity functions as a geo-political marker.

The Greco-Turkish War from 1919 to 1923 and subsequent population exchanges redrew Greece's ethnic and religious geography. They displaced hundreds of thousands and cemented the national population.

Strategically located at the Mediterranean's northeastern approach, with control over the Dardanelles shared with Turkey and access to the Black Sea, Greece is vital to NATO Mediterranean strategy.
